query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning–augmented adaptive enhanced sampling scheme, trained on targeted ab initio datasets, can efficiently and accurately compute the full free-energy landscapes (accounting for vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling) of solid and liquid phases near fusion temperatures, reducing computational cost by 10–100× compared to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD methods while maintaining fidelity within about 5% deviation in key metrics.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys in their equilibrium solid or liquid states near fusion conditions.
generation.intervention: Replace fully dynamical ab initio MD simulations with an adaptive enhanced sampling framework that deploys ML potentials as surrogates for expensive force evaluations, with periodic ab initio recalibration to ensure retention of all relevant free-energy contributions.
generation.conditions: Applied to both solid and fluid phases in systems at temperatures near their melting points (e.g., from ~0.8Tm up to Tm). Initial validation in elemental and binary systems is extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys where direct methods are computationally prohibitive.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential acts as an efficient surrogate model embedded within an adaptive enhanced sampling algorithm (e.g., umbrella sampling or metadynamics), ensuring that the statistical mechanical treatment correctly captures stacking, polymorphism, and anharmonic effects.
generation.mechanism: The ML model, trained on a judiciously chosen ab initio dataset, is used to navigate complex phase spaces rapidly while periodic ab initio corrections keep errors in vibrational entropy, electron–vibration coupling, and anharmonicity low. This adaptive scheme maintains high fidelity in computed free energies of both phases and thus the derived fusion properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method should yield phase free energies and fusion temperature estimates that deviate less than approximately 5% from those obtained via explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD. Additionally, the computational speed is predicted to be 10–100 times faster due to the efficiency of the ML surrogate and adaptive sampling.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation via molecular dynamics and the TOR-TILD method as validated on elemental and binary systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to perform well for systems ranging from elemental and binary alloys to complex, multicomponent high-entropy alloys, particularly near fusion temperatures. It may need further refinement for systems with extreme anharmonicity or electron–vibration coupling beyond the training dataset’s scope.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the transferability of ML potentials across different compositions and phases, especially for capturing subtle free-energy contributions in complex high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of comparative free-energy calculations on a well-characterized elemental or binary system and on a representative high-entropy alloy. The experiment should run three parallel workflows: (i) explicit ab initio MD-based free-energy evaluation, (ii) TOR-TILD, and (iii) the proposed ML-augmented adaptive enhanced sampling method with periodic ab initio recalibration. The free-energy curves, fusion temperatures, and derived observables (e.g., latent heat) from each method will be directly compared.
measurements: Free energy curves for both solid and liquid states
Statistical convergence metrics (error bars) for sampled observables
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-augmented method produces phase free energies or fusion temperatures that differ by more than ~5% from the explicitly computed ab initio MD results or TOR-TILD benchmarks, or if convergence issues indicate a loss of fidelity in capturing the entropy contributions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

chosen.conditions: applied to both solid and liquid states in multicomponent high-entropy alloys near fusion temperatures, ensuring full retention of vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling
chosen.why: Prior studies show that explicit ab initio MD, although accurate, is computationally prohibitive, and TOR-TILD, while effective for simpler systems, becomes too slow for multicomponent alloys. By training ML potentials on a curated ab initio dataset and using them in an adaptive enhanced sampling framework, the method is anticipated to achieve similar fidelity (within, e.g., 5% deviation in phase free energies and melting temperatures) at a fraction (potentially 10–100× speedup) of the computational cost. Benchmarking against established elemental and binary results (e.g., known free-energy curves and phase transition observables) will decisively test the method’s validity, with significant deviation from these references falsifying the hypothesis.
